title: In-Situ 4D-STEM Mapping of Crystalline Orientation and 3D Topology of Gold Nanorods in Liquid Phase
content: In-situ liquid phase transmission electron microscopy (LPTEM) is a key approach for directly visualizing morphological evolution and resolving dynamic processes at heterogeneous interfaces under reactive conditions, with broad applications ranging from catalysis, batteries to imaging beam-sensitive biological specimens such as proteins and enzymes in their native aqueous environments [1,2]. Here, we integrate a nanochannel liquid cell with four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) to investigate self-assembled gold (Au) nanorods immersed in water (Fig. 1a). Utilizing in situ 4D-STEM, we map nanoscale heterogeneities, including preferential crystalline orientation, long-range ordering, and 3D topology of Au nanorods in liquid phase. This methodology can be adapted for structural biology applications, facilitating the direct visualization of conformational dynamics and self-assembly of proteins and peptides in their native environments with high spatiotemporal resolution under low-dose imaging conditions.
